title: Terminology Crimes
intro: The words that cost hours. Misnomers, legacy names and false friends that make correct work sound wrong and wrong work sound obvious. Ranked by the damage they do.

crime_types.misnomer: The name asserts something false or value-laden about the thing.
crime_types.legacy: A historical accident outlived the theory that produced it.
crime_types.metaphor: A figure of speech is read as a literal property.
crime_types.false-friend: An everyday synonym hides a technical inversion.
crime_types.overloaded: One word is forced to do several incompatible jobs.
crime_types.opaque: The name encodes no meaning at all; it must be memorized.

crimes.damage: Turns “not a bell curve” into “bad data”, so teams transform first and ask later.
crimes.sounds_like: The default, healthy, standard shape every dataset should have.
crimes.actually_means: A specific symmetric bell curve defined by its mean and variance — the Gaussian distribution.
crimes.trap: Most real data — income, latency, traffic — is skewed, heavy-tailed or multimodal. The name supplies a false baseline and makes the actual distribution look like a defect.
crimes.use_instead: Gaussian (and name the distribution you actually have).

sources.label: Stigler, S. M. (1986). The History of Statistics.

crimes.damage: Sounds like decay, so people miss that it is just fitting a relationship.
crimes.sounds_like: Going backward, reverting, getting worse.
crimes.actually_means: Modelling a dependent variable as a function of one or more predictors.
crimes.trap: Galton coined “regression toward mediocrity” for an observed genetic phenomenon, not for the method. The word now hides linear, logistic, quantile and every other model family.
crimes.use_instead: Fit / model — and name the model (linear regression, logistic regression).

sources.label: Galton, F. (1886). Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature.

crimes.damage: Turns the benchmark into a straw man; “reject at all costs” is how p-hacking starts.
crimes.sounds_like: An empty hypothesis, a worthless idea, or a hypothesis stating that everything equals zero.
crimes.actually_means: A baseline reference model — no effect, no difference, default noise — against which the data are compared.
crimes.trap: “Null” sounds dismissive, so H₀ becomes the villain rather than the benchmark. Rejecting it says the data are unlikely under the baseline; it does not prove your alternative.
crimes.use_instead: Baseline hypothesis / reference model.

sources.label: Fisher, R. A. (1925). Statistical Methods for Research Workers.

crimes.term: Type I and Type II Errors
crimes.damage: Two labels with zero semantics; people mix them up mid-sentence and misreport risk.
crimes.sounds_like: Error 1 and Error 2 on a system status panel.
crimes.actually_means: Type I = false positive: reject a true H₀. Type II = false negative: fail to reject a false H₀.
crimes.trap: Roman numerals carry no meaning, and they hide the asymmetry: Type I is set by α, Type II by power. Swap the words and you swap the risk.
crimes.use_instead: False positive / false negative (α error / β error when you mean the rates).

sources.label: Neyman, J., & Pearson, E. S. (1933). On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses.
Wikipedia: Type I and type II errors

crimes.damage: Makes an impossible value sound like a forecast, then the model gets blamed when 3.5 never shows up.
crimes.sounds_like: The single value you should expect to see when you run an experiment.
crimes.actually_means: The probability-weighted mean over all realizations — a long-run average, not a prediction.
crimes.trap: The expected value of a die is 3.5; you will never roll it. For skewed distributions it can sit where no observation can.
crimes.use_instead: Mean / probability-weighted average (or “long-run average”).

sources.label: Casella, G., & Berger, R. L. (2002). Statistical Inference.

crimes.damage: Launders non-normal data into “normal” in people's heads, then produces bogus t-tests and confidence intervals.
crimes.sounds_like: A central law saying large datasets collapse to a point or become normal.
crimes.actually_means: The normalized sum or average of independent, finite-variance variables tends to a Gaussian as n grows — the sampling distribution of the mean, not the raw data.
crimes.trap: The data do not become normal. Only the standardized mean's distribution approaches normal; dependence, heavy tails and infinite variance break the guarantee.
crimes.use_instead: CLT for the sampling distribution of the mean (check the assumptions).

sources.label: Casella, G., & Berger, R. L. (2002). Statistical Inference.

crimes.damage: Reverses the condition in your head and produces confident P(θ | data) nonsense.
crimes.sounds_like: Synonyms for how probable something is.
crimes.actually_means: Probability fixes the parameter and measures data: P(data | θ). Likelihood fixes the observed data and measures the parameter: L(θ; data).
crimes.trap: Everyday English treats them as interchangeable. Swapping the fixed side turns a density into a function of parameters; a likelihood is not a probability distribution over θ.
crimes.use_instead: Probability of the data given θ; likelihood of θ given the data.

sources.label: Fisher, R. A. (1922). On the mathematical foundations of theoretical statistics.

crimes.damage: Sounds dead, so people detrend and filter a process that is only statistically stable.
crimes.sounds_like: A process standing still, not moving, dead in the water.
crimes.actually_means: A stochastic process whose joint distribution — mean, variance, autocovariance — does not change with time.
crimes.trap: A stationary series can jump every millisecond. Stationarity is a property of the generating law, not of the realised values; it says nothing about how boring the plot looks.
crimes.use_instead: Distributionally stable / time-invariant law (strict or weak, as the case may be).

sources.label: Hamilton, J. D. (1994). Time Series Analysis.

crimes.damage: Sells a point estimate as the most probable parameter, then everyone forgets the prior.
crimes.sounds_like: The parameter with the highest probability of being true.
crimes.actually_means: The θ that maximizes the probability or density of the observed data — the argmax of L(θ; data).
crimes.trap: An MLE is not P(θ | data). Without a prior it is not a posterior; it is the setting under which the data look least surprising. It can be biased, boundary-invalid, or non-identifiable.
crimes.use_instead: Maximum-likelihood estimate (the θ that makes the data most likely).

sources.label: Fisher, R. A. (1922). On the mathematical foundations of theoretical statistics.

crimes.damage: Sounds like cleaning or repairing, so nobody states the transform and everyone assumes the shape changed.
crimes.sounds_like: Standardizing to an accepted rule, cleaning messy data, or making it normal.
crimes.actually_means: z = (x − μ) / σ: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation; dimensionless, mean 0, sd 1.
crimes.trap: “Normalization” does not make data normal; “standardization” does not fix formatting. Location and scale change; skew, tails and shape survive untouched.
crimes.use_instead: z-scored / rescaled — and write the transform.

sources.label: Casella, G., & Berger, R. L. (2002). Statistical Inference.

crimes.damage: Makes a deterministic function sound like a dice roll, so nobody can say what is actually random.
crimes.sounds_like: A variable that is random — a quantity whose value is unpredictable.
crimes.actually_means: A measurable function from a sample space to a value space, X: Ω → ℝ. The randomness belongs to the outcome ω, not to X; given ω, X(ω) is fixed.
crimes.trap: A random variable is neither random nor a variable in the algebraic sense. Confusing it with its distribution hides that different variables can share one distribution, and that P(X = x) can be zero for continuous X.
crimes.use_instead: Measurable function on outcomes — and say “its distribution” when you mean the law.

sources.label: Kolmogorov, A. N. (1933). Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung.
Casella, G., & Berger, R. L. (2002). Statistical Inference.

crimes.damage: Lets people read density values as probabilities, then wonder why a density of 3 is “300%”.
crimes.sounds_like: The probability of each value of a continuous variable.
crimes.actually_means: A function f such that probabilities are integrals over intervals; f(x) is density per unit x, not P(X = x).
crimes.trap: A density can exceed 1 and carries units of inverse x. Only its integral over a set is a probability; for continuous X, P(X = x) = 0.
crimes.use_instead: Density — integrate over an interval to get probability.

sources.label: Casella, G., & Berger, R. L. (2002). Statistical Inference.

crimes.damage: Turns a coverage procedure into a 95% probability claim; the number is then quoted as if it were a posterior.
crimes.sounds_like: There is a 95% probability that the true value lies in this interval.
crimes.actually_means: A procedure that, over repeated samples, covers the true parameter 95% of the time under its assumptions.
crimes.trap: A realised interval either contains the value or not; the 95% is a property of the procedure, not of this interval. Coverage is not the probability that the parameter is inside, and it depends on the model being right.
crimes.use_instead: 95% confidence procedure — report the interval and its coverage.

sources.label: Neyman, J. (1937). Outline of a theory of statistical estimation based on the classical theory of probability.

crimes.damage: The most misquoted number in science: read as P(H0 | data) and used as a truth machine.
crimes.sounds_like: The probability that the null hypothesis is true, or that the result is due to chance.
crimes.actually_means: The probability, under H0 and the model, of a result at least as extreme as the observed one.
crimes.trap: P(data | H0) is not P(H0 | data). A small p-value says the data are surprising under the baseline; it does not measure effect size, importance, or the probability of replication.
crimes.use_instead: p-value = P(data at least this extreme | H0) — report the effect and interval.

sources.label: Wasserstein, R. L., & Lazar, N. A. (2016). The ASA statement on p-values.
Greenland, S., et al. (2016). Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power.

crimes.damage: Makes “significant” sound important, certain, or large; then significant noise gets shipped.
crimes.sounds_like: The result is important, reliable, or practically meaningful.
crimes.actually_means: The observed result is unlikely under a specified null model at a chosen threshold.
crimes.trap: Significance is a relation between data and a null, not a property of the effect. With enough data, trivial effects become significant; with too little, large ones do not.
crimes.use_instead: Statistically detectable under this null — report effect size and interval.

sources.label: Wasserstein, R. L., Schirm, A. L., & Lazar, N. A. (2019). Moving to a world beyond “p < 0.05”.

crimes.damage: Sounds like a mistake, so people report it as if it were a standard deviation of the data.
crimes.sounds_like: An error in the standard, or the standard deviation of the sample.
crimes.actually_means: The standard deviation of an estimator’s sampling distribution — how much the estimate would vary across repeated samples.
crimes.trap: The standard error is not the SD of the data and not an error. It shrinks with √n; for a mean it is s/√n, and it says nothing about bias.
crimes.use_instead: Standard error of the estimate — the SD of its sampling distribution.

sources.label: Casella, G., & Berger, R. L. (2002). Statistical Inference.

crimes.damage: Sounds like freedom; hides the constraint count that sets the denominator of every test.
crimes.sounds_like: How free the data are — an abstract allowance.
crimes.actually_means: The number of independent pieces of information left after estimating constraints (e.g., n − 1 after estimating a mean).
crimes.trap: Degrees of freedom are not a mood; they are a bookkeeping count of independent deviations. Getting them wrong silently changes p-values and intervals.
crimes.use_instead: Residual degrees of freedom — count of independent pieces after constraints.

crimes.damage: Sounds like strength or authority; underpowered studies then get read as evidence of no effect.
crimes.sounds_like: The strength of a test or of a result.
crimes.actually_means: The probability of rejecting H0 when H0 is false — 1 − β, at a specified alternative and sample size.
crimes.trap: Power is a property of the test, the alternative and the design, not of the observed result. A non-significant result from an underpowered study is not evidence for H0.
crimes.use_instead: Power against this alternative (1 − β) — report the minimum detectable effect.

sources.label: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences.

crimes.damage: Everyday prejudice and statistical bias share a word, so a biased estimator gets treated as a moral failure.
crimes.sounds_like: Prejudice, unfairness, or a distorted view.
crimes.actually_means: For an estimator, E[θ̂] − θ: the average deviation of the estimate from the target over repeated samples.
crimes.trap: A biased estimator can be useful (low MSE), and an unbiased one can be terrible (huge variance). Bias is one component of error, not a verdict on the method.
crimes.use_instead: Estimator bias E[θ̂] − θ — report variance/MSE alongside.

sources.label: Casella, G., & Berger, R. L. (2002). Statistical Inference.

crimes.damage: Read as “any relationship” or “causation”, then linear-association numbers drive causal stories.
crimes.sounds_like: How strongly two things are related — or that one causes the other.
crimes.actually_means: A measure of linear association between two variables (Pearson) or a rank/other association (Spearman, etc.).
crimes.trap: Zero correlation does not mean independence; nonzero correlation does not mean causation. The coefficient also depends on the range and on outliers.
crimes.use_instead: Linear association — state the coefficient; causality needs a design.

sources.label: Pearson, K. (1895). Notes on regression and inheritance in the case of two parents.

crimes.damage: Makes a variance decomposition sound like a causal explanation; R² becomes the score of the model’s understanding.
crimes.sounds_like: How much of the phenomenon the model explains.
crimes.actually_means: The proportion of the response’s variance accounted for by the fitted model: 1 − SS_res / SS_tot.
crimes.trap: Explained variance is a fit statistic, not an explanation. R² rises with extra predictors, depends on the sample’s range, and says nothing about mechanism or out-of-sample skill.
crimes.use_instead: Proportion of variance accounted for (R²) — validate out of sample.

crimes.damage: Turns a fallible reference label into metaphysical truth, then every error is charged to the model.
crimes.sounds_like: The actual, certain, objective state of the world.
crimes.actually_means: The reference labels or measurements used to score a model — themselves produced by a protocol, an instrument, or annotators.
crimes.trap: Ground truth is operational, not absolute. If the reference is noisy or biased, the model is scored against the error, and “accuracy” measures agreement with the protocol.
crimes.use_instead: Reference standard / evaluation labels — state how they were produced.

crimes.damage: Suggests “no parameters”; people then expect a model-free miracle and are surprised by smoothing choices.
crimes.sounds_like: A method with no parameters at all.
crimes.actually_means: A model whose parameter space is infinite-dimensional or distribution-free — it still has tuning or smoothing parameters.
crimes.trap: Nonparametric does not mean assumption-free or parameter-free. Kernel bandwidths, spline penalties and tree depths are parameters; they just do not index a fixed finite family.
crimes.use_instead: Distribution-free / infinite-dimensional model — name the tuning parameters.

crimes.damage: A four-letter assumption that gets waved through when dependence is the whole problem.
crimes.sounds_like: Independent and identically distributed — a harmless default.
crimes.actually_means: The observations are mutually independent and share one distribution; independence is probabilistic, not causal.
crimes.trap: i.i.d. is a modelling assumption, not a description of the data. Time series, clustered data and network data violate it; the standard errors and tests that assume it then lie.
crimes.use_instead: i.i.d. — state it and test it; otherwise model the dependence.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Independent and identically distributed random variables

crimes.damage: Sounds like “any sample” or “arbitrary sample”; selection bias then hides behind the word random.
crimes.sounds_like: A sample that happened by chance, or any sample taken without a rule.
crimes.actually_means: A sample drawn by a specified probabilistic mechanism that gives known inclusion probabilities.
crimes.trap: Random does not mean haphazard. A convenience sample is not a random sample; without the sampling mechanism, uncertainty statements lose their warrant.
crimes.use_instead: Probability sample — state the sampling design.

crimes.damage: Sounds like the Bayesian twin of a confidence interval, so people assume the same guarantee — or that it is automatically better.
crimes.sounds_like: An interval you can believe: the parameter is probably inside it.
crimes.actually_means: A posterior interval: given the prior and likelihood, the parameter lies in it with the stated posterior probability.
crimes.trap: A 95% credible interval is 95% conditional on the prior and model. It is not a frequentist coverage guarantee, and an overconfident prior makes it narrow for the wrong reason. The two intervals answer different questions.
crimes.use_instead: Posterior credible interval — state the prior.

sources.label: Gelman, A., et al. (2013). Bayesian Data Analysis.

crimes.damage: The temporal metaphor (“before/after”) hides that a prior is a modelling choice, not a timestamp.
crimes.sounds_like: Prior = before the data, posterior = after; the data automatically correct the prior.
crimes.actually_means: Prior: a distribution over parameters before the likelihood is applied. Posterior: the distribution after conditioning on data, proportional to prior × likelihood.
crimes.trap: The prior is not “before” in time when it is chosen after seeing the data, and a posterior is not objective just because it is “after”. Priors encode assumptions; with weak data the posterior is the prior in disguise.
crimes.use_instead: Parameter prior / posterior — state the model and the prior.

sources.label: Gelman, A., et al. (2013). Bayesian Data Analysis.

crimes.damage: A five-syllable word for “time average equals ensemble average”; teams assume it and then estimate a trend from one path.
crimes.sounds_like: Something about energy or work (ergonomics?).
crimes.actually_means: A property whereby long-run time averages of one realisation converge to ensemble averages under the process law.
crimes.trap: Ergodicity is not stationarity, and it is not automatic. A process can be stationary but not ergodic; if it is not ergodic, one long run tells you about one path, not the ensemble.
crimes.use_instead: Ergodic (time averages = ensemble averages) — say why it holds.

sources.label: Hamilton, J. D. (1994). Time Series Analysis.

crimes.damage: “Sufficient statistic” sounds like “enough data”, so people think it means a large sample rather than a compression.
crimes.sounds_like: A statistic that is sufficient — enough to do the job.
crimes.actually_means: A statistic T(X) is sufficient for θ if the distribution of X given T does not depend on θ: it retains all information about θ.
crimes.trap: Sufficiency is about information loss, not sample size. A sufficient statistic can be one number; a large sample of an insufficient statistic still loses information.
crimes.use_instead: Sufficient statistic — no information about θ lost.

sources.label: Casella, G., & Berger, R. L. (2002). Statistical Inference.

crimes.damage: “Unbiased” sounds fair, “efficient” sounds fast; both are technical and can trade against each other.
crimes.sounds_like: Unbiased = fair; efficient = quick or cheap; so both are always good.
crimes.actually_means: Unbiased: E[θ̂] = θ. Efficient: low variance (relative to a bound or another estimator), often asymptotically.
crimes.trap: An unbiased estimator can have huge variance; a biased one can have lower MSE. Efficiency is about variance, not speed. “Best unbiased” is a constrained optimum, not a universal one.
crimes.use_instead: Unbiased (E[θ̂] = θ) and minimum-variance / efficient — state the class.

sources.label: Casella, G., & Berger, R. L. (2002). Statistical Inference.

crimes.damage: “Robust” sounds strong; it hides to what the method is robust and how much efficiency it pays.
crimes.sounds_like: Strong, reliable, works under everything.
crimes.actually_means: Insensitive (bounded influence) to specified deviations — outliers, heavy tails, model misspecification — usually at some efficiency cost.
crimes.trap: Robustness is relative to a contamination model. A robust estimator can fail under a different violation, and the word is used as a free pass for unexamined assumptions.
crimes.use_instead: Robust to [outliers/heavy tails/…] under [model] — report the efficiency cost.

sources.label: Huber, P. J., & Ronchetti, E. M. (2009). Robust Statistics.

crimes.damage: “Random” and “fixed” sound like chance versus certainty; the real distinction is conditional versus marginal and exchangeable grouping.
crimes.sounds_like: Random effect = a variable that varies randomly; fixed effect = a constant.
crimes.actually_means: Random effect: group-level coefficients modelled as draws from a distribution (exchangeable). Fixed effect: group-specific parameters estimated without that distributional assumption.
crimes.trap: A fixed effect is not fixed in value; a random effect is not random in the dice sense. The choice changes the estimand, the shrinkage, and the interpretation.
crimes.use_instead: Group-level (random) effect with a distributional assumption; group-specific (fixed) effect.

sources.label: Gelman, A., & Hill, J. (2007). Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models.

crimes.damage: “Instrument” sounds like a measurement tool; it is actually an external variable used to isolate causal variation.
crimes.sounds_like: A tool or instrument used to measure the variable.
crimes.actually_means: A variable Z that affects treatment X but affects outcome Y only through X (exclusion restriction), used to identify a causal effect when X is endogenous.
crimes.trap: The name suggests measurement; validity rests on relevance and exclusion, not on the instrument being a better measurement. A weak or invalid instrument is worse than no instrument.
crimes.use_instead: Instrument Z — state relevance and exclusion.

sources.label: Angrist, J. D., & Pischke, J.-S. (2009). Mostly Harmless Econometrics.

crimes.damage: Sounds like “internal to the system”; it actually means the regressor is correlated with the error, so OLS is biased.
crimes.sounds_like: The variable is endogenous — internal, naturally arising.
crimes.actually_means: Cov(X, ε) ≠ 0: the regressor is correlated with the unobserved error, so the estimator does not recover the causal effect.
crimes.trap: Endogeneity is not “the variable comes from inside the model”. It is a failure of exogeneity; the fix (instrument, control, design) must address the specific correlation.
crimes.use_instead: Regressor–error dependence — state the source (omitted variable, simultaneity, measurement error).

sources.label: Wooldridge, J. M. (2010). Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data.

crimes.damage: Greek for “different scatter”; people treat it as a disease rather than a property that changes the right standard errors.
crimes.sounds_like: Something exotic and bad — hetero-skedastic.
crimes.actually_means: The conditional variance of the error is not constant across observations: Var(ε | X) varies.
crimes.trap: Heteroskedasticity does not necessarily bias OLS coefficients; it invalidates the usual standard errors. The fix is robust/clustered inference or a different model, not necessarily a transformation.
crimes.use_instead: Non-constant error variance — use robust or clustered SEs.

sources.label: White, H. (1980). A heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance matrix estimator.

crimes.damage: Sounds like harmless background; it is a precise moment assumption routinely assumed and rarely checked.
crimes.sounds_like: Random static — harmless, structureless noise.
crimes.actually_means: A sequence with zero mean, constant variance and no serial correlation (weak white noise); strong white noise adds independence and identical distribution.
crimes.trap: White noise is not “any noise”. Uncorrelatedness is not independence; a process can be white in the weak sense yet dependent nonlinearly, and financial “noise” is rarely white.
crimes.use_instead: Serially uncorrelated (weak white noise) — specify the moment conditions.

sources.label: Hamilton, J. D. (1994). Time Series Analysis.

crimes.damage: A dramatic metaphor that hides the actual scaling: distances concentrate, volume vanishes, and sample requirements explode.
crimes.sounds_like: Dimensions are cursed — mysterious bad luck in high dimensions.
crimes.actually_means: The family of failures of intuition and sample-based methods as dimension grows: data become sparse, distances concentrate, and nonparametric rates degrade exponentially.
crimes.trap: It is not one theorem or one curse; different methods fail differently. The fix is structure (sparsity, manifolds, priors), not more of the same data.
crimes.use_instead: High-dimensional scaling failure — name the mechanism (sparsity, distance concentration, sample complexity).

sources.label: Bellman, R. E. (1961). Adaptive Control Processes.
